Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a **high‑level workflow** you could follow if you had two generic tools at your disposal: | Step | What you need to do | Why it matters | Example of what the tool might return | |------|---------------------|----------------|---------------------------------------| | **1. Find the right API** | Use the *search* tool to locate an official or third‑party API that lets you place a McDonald’s order. | You need a documented endpoint that accepts menu selections, location, payment, etc. | `search("McDonald's ordering API") → {"endpoint": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/order", "docs": "..."}` | **2. Inspect the API contract** | Pull the OpenAPI/Swagger spec or read the docs to learn:
• Authentication method (OAuth, API key, JWT, etc.)
• Required headers
• Payload schema (menu IDs, quantity, modifiers)
• Order‑creation endpoint, status endpoint, payment endpoint | Knowing the contract lets you build a valid request. | `search("McDonald's order API spec") → {"auth": "OAuth2", "menu_endpoint": "/menu", "order_endpoint": "/orders"}` | **3. Authenticate** | Call the auth endpoint (or use a pre‑obtained token) to get a bearer token or session cookie. | Without a token you can’t place an order. | `execute("POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/auth/login {\"email\":\"you@example.com\",\"password\":\"•••\"}") → {"access_token":"eyJhbGciOi…"}` | **4. Resolve menu items** | Query the menu endpoint to find the IDs for “burger” and “fries”. | The API usually expects numeric IDs, not text. | `execute("GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu") → {"items":[{"id":101,"name":"Burger"},{"id":202,"name":"Fries"}]}` | **5. Build the order payload** | Create a JSON body that lists the items, quantities, any modifiers, and the delivery/pick‑up location. | The payload must match the schema. | ```json { "location": {"lat": 40.7128, "lon": -74.0060}, "items":[{"id":101,"qty":1},{"id":202,"qty":1}], "delivery":true } ``` | | **6. Place the order** | Send a POST to the order endpoint with the bearer token in the `Authorization` header. | This is the actual “order” action. | `execute("POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders {payload} -H \"Authorization: Bearer \"") → {"order_id":"abc123","status":"pending"}` | **7. Attach payment** | If the API separates payment, call the payment endpoint with card details or a stored payment method. | The order won’t complete until paid. | `execute("POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders/abc123/pay {payment_info}") → {"status":"paid"}` | **8. Confirm & track** | Poll the status endpoint or subscribe to a webhook to get updates (ready, out for delivery, etc.). | Gives you real‑time feedback. | `execute("GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/orders/abc123") → {"status":"delivered"}` --- ### Putting it together in pseudo‑code ```python # 1. Search for the API api_info = search("McDonald's ordering API") endpoint = api_info["endpoint"] # 2. Authenticate auth_resp = execute(f"POST {endpoint}/auth/login {{\"email\":\"you@example.com\",\"password\":\"•••\"}}") token = auth_resp["access_token"] # 3. Get menu IDs menu = execute(f"GET {endpoint}/menu") burger_id = next(i["id"] for i in menu["items"] if i["name"] == "Burger") fries_id = next(i["id"] for i in menu["items"] if i["name"] == "Fries") # 4. Build order order_payload = { "location": {"lat": 40.7128, "lon": -74.0060}, "items": [{"id": burger_id, "qty": 1}, {"id": fries_id, "qty": 1}], "delivery": True } # 5. Place order order_resp = execute( f"POST {endpoint}/orders {order_payload} -H \"Authorization: Bearer {token}\"" ) order_id = order_resp["order_id"] # 6. Pay payment_info = {"card_number":"4111111111111111","exp":"12/25","cvv":"123"} pay_resp = execute(f"POST {endpoint}/orders/{order_id}/pay {payment_info}") # 7. Track status = execute(f"GET {endpoint}/orders/{order_id}") print(status["status"]) ``` --- ### Things to watch out for | Issue | Mitigation | |-------|------------| | **Rate limits / throttling** | Respect `Retry-After` headers; back‑off if needed. | | **Location restrictions** | Verify the coordinates are within a McDonald’s service area. | | **Payment security** | Never log raw card numbers; use PCI‑compliant tokenization if the API supports it. | | **Error handling** | Check HTTP status codes; parse error messages; retry on transient failures. | | **User consent** | Ensure you have the user’s permission to use their payment info and location. | --- ### Bottom line 1. **Search** → find the API docs. 2. **Read** → understand auth, menu, order, payment flows. 3. **Execute** → call the endpoints in the correct order (auth → menu → order → pay → track). With those two tools you can programmatically place a burger and fries order for McDonald’s, as long as the restaurant exposes a suitable API (or you go through a delivery partner’s API).
